activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: In his Rhetoric, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence.
story:
The essay was due Friday morning, and it was already Wednesday, which was why Eva was sitting at the back table of the public library with three books, a granola bar, and a growing pile of crumpled paper. Her teacher, Mr. Park, wanted a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction, a conclusion, and, he had said twice, actual convincing. Eva knew how to argue; she argued with her brother about everything. But every time she tried to write "I believe the school should have a chess club," it came out flat, like a cereal box talking.

Her friend Nimrat slid into the chair across from her, holding her own finished essay like a trophy. Eva tried not to envy her, and failed completely. "What's your secret?" Eva asked. Nimrat shrugged. "I just wrote stuff. Mr. Park liked it." That was the part that stung. Nimrat hadn't even tried, and it had worked. Eva flipped through her library books, hunting through the article database on the library computer for anything about how to change people's minds, until a photocopy of an old page gave her three strange words: ethos, pathos, logos. She copied them onto her hand.

That evening her grandfather picked her up, saw the words on her skin, and laughed. "Ethos, pathos, logos," he said. "Aristotle, in his Rhetoric. Three ways to persuade: ethos is the speaker's credibility, pathos is the audience's emotions, and logos is logic and evidence." He tapped her hand. "A Greek philosopher beat your essay deadline by a couple of years."

Eva stayed up late testing it. Ethos: Mr. Park should trust her because she had run the chess booth at the school fair. Pathos: kids eating lunch alone with nobody to play a game with. Logos: chess improves memory, and the library already owned four boards nobody used. She remembered, guiltily, the time she'd told her brother the vacuum was broken so he'd do her chore, and how it had worked for a week and then stopped forever. That was pathos with no logos, she decided. A trick instead of a reason. Or maybe she was still deciding.

Thursday night, Danika texted her: "our class voted on club ideas today. chess got zero votes." Eva stared at the phone, then typed back, "my essay is tomorrow. want to bet?" Danika sent back a single eyes emoji. On Friday, Eva read her five paragraphs out loud, slow, watching Mr. Park's eyebrows go up at the lunch-lunch-alone part. After class, the whole group was unanimous: one more vote, next Friday, after everyone read her essay posted on the door. Danika found her at her locker. "You owe me nothing," Eva said, "yet."

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Plant cells are joined by tiny channels through their walls called plasmodesmata, which let materials pass directly from one cell to the next.
story:
Felix crouched between the rows of tomato plants at Ms. Morningstar's farm, holding a microscope slide he had pressed from the thin skin of an onion she had given him. His science project was due in two days, and the task on the worksheet was one he had read so many times he could recite it in his sleep: compare a plant cell and an animal cell, and name the parts only plants have. He had drawn animal cells already, from the cheek cells Armin had stained for him at school. Those cells looked like fried eggs, round and soft, with no wall around them at all.

The onion cells were different. Under the lens they lay in straight bricklike rows, each one boxed in by a robust wall that caught the light like a fence. Cell wall, Felix wrote. Chloroplasts, which the animal cells didn't have either. But as he watched, an old question came back to him, the same one he'd had at the science museum last spring, when he and Mehtab had built a plant cell model out of foam and Felix had stared at it and wondered how cells trapped inside walls could share anything.

He found a spot where two walls met and turned the fine focus, holding his breath out of reflex, as if moving might shake the cells apart. There, faint as a thread, was a tiny gap crossing the wall between one cell and the next. He thought of the museum docent's voice fading off before she'd answered him, and how he'd never asked again. He should have asked. He'd been too worried his question was dumb.

"Ms. Morningstar!" he called across the beds. She came over, wiping dirt from her hands, and bent to the eyepiece. "What do you call this? It's like a tunnel through the wall."

"Plasmodesmata," she said. "They permit materials to pass directly from one cell to the next."

Felix printed the word carefully at the bottom of his drawing, then drew a small arrow through the wall and labeled it. "Mehtab is going to flip," he said.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder.
story:
Megan counted the money twice before she left: one five-dollar bill, three quarters, and a dime, in case the milk cost more than the last time. "Get two liters," her mom said from the couch, "and check the change before you leave the store." The corner store was four blocks away, and Megan had walked partway there a hundred times, but never the whole way alone, never with money in her own pocket.

Mr. Delgado was sweeping the sidewalk outside his shop next door. "First solo run?" he asked, and Megan nodded. "Bring me back the price and I'll tell you if you got a fair deal." Inside the store, she found the milk, watched the register climb to $4.29, and handed over the five. The cashier gave her two quarters, two dimes, and a penny. Megan counted it on the counter, converting the coins in her head until she was sure: 71 cents. That was right.

When she got home, her mom poured a little into a glass and frowned. "This smells off already. That's the second carton this week." Megan sniffed it and agreed, sour. She carried the second carton to the fridge and stood in front of the open door, thinking. Two cartons going bad early wasn't bad luck, it was a pattern, and a pattern meant something was causing it. She found the dial inside, set somewhere in the middle, and beside it a small thermometer she'd never noticed. It read 46 degrees.

Megan remembered a poster from the nurse's office: food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or colder. This fridge was warmer than that. She turned the dial and watched the number creep down until it read 38. "Diagnosis," she announced when her mom looked over. "The fridge, not the store." Her mom laughed. "Smart girl. And your brother's sniffles aren't contagious, so tomorrow you can go back for eggs." Megan put the milk on the shelf and slid the thermometer to the front where she could see it.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The argument started over a display board in the hallway outside the gym, where students were pinning up photos and short paragraphs about their families for International Week. Toby read Lily-Anne's card, which said her family was Anishinaabe on her grandmother's side, and shook his head. "You can't just put that," he said. "You don't even live on a reserve. My uncle says you have to be on the official list, or you're not really anything." Lily-Anne's ears went pink, and she pulled the card off the board and crumpled it. "It's not your uncle's card," she said, and walked away down the hall.

Gabriella found her at lunch, sitting alone at the end of the long table, drawing knots on her brown paper bag with a pen. Gabriella sat down and unwrapped her sandwich slowly, because she had learned that Lily-Anne talked better when nobody asked her anything right away. "I don't even know if I believe him," Lily-Anne finally said. "But he sounded so sure." Gabriella thought about that all through afternoon class, turning it over. Toby's uncle wasn't the boss of anything, as far as she knew. But she couldn't see who actually was the boss of it either, and that was the real problem: the rule, if there was one, was invisible. So she decided to test the simplest idea she had, which was that somebody, somewhere, had written the rule down.

In the library, while Ms. Moose shelved books about gardening and muttered about an invasive vine that had strangled half the flowerbed by the front door, Gabriella took the computer by the window. She typed question after question, badly at first, then better. She found a page about the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, which had been adopted on 13 September 2007. She read the line twice, then a third time, to make sure she had it right, and copied it onto her hand because her notebook was in her locker.

She caught up with the two of them at once, near the water fountain, because that seemed fairest. "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007," she read off her palm, "says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership." Toby frowned. "So who decides if Lily-Anne counts?" "Not your uncle," Gabriella said. Lily-Anne looked at the smudged ink on Gabriella's hand and began to smile, slowly, like a door opening. "Can I copy that onto a new card?" she asked. "Bigger letters this time."

Toby was quiet the rest of the afternoon, and the next morning he was waiting by the display board with a fresh sheet of tape in his hand. "I told my uncle he was wrong," he said. "He said fine, but somebody has to sustain an argument with better evidence than ink on your hand." Gabriella held the tape while Lily-Anne smoothed the new card flat, right at the centre of the board, where nobody could miss it.

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron, so almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
story:
Muhammad had claimed the garage as his science workshop, mostly because it smelled like sawdust and nobody bothered him there. On the workbench lay a note Ms. Wu had slipped him after class, and he read it again for the tenth time. "Dear Muhammad," it said, "your sketch of the carbon atom was lovely, but check the masses before you build. Curiosity is the best teacher, so I will say no more. Yours, Ms. Wu." He frowned at the paper. The sketch had looked perfect to him, a fat nucleus and six electrons, all drawn as circles the same size.

Giuliano arrived first, carrying a bag of marbles, and Sehaj came next with a box of peppercorns and a roll of fishing line. "Okay," Muhammad said, holding up his notebook, "Ms. Wu says something's wrong with my sizes. Six protons, six neutrons, six electrons. Carbon. Easy." Giuliano dumped the marbles out. "We use marbles for everything. Atoms are made of little balls, right?" Sehaj picked up a peppercorn and squinted at it. "Except electrons aren't really little balls. They're more like fuzzy clouds." "Fuzzy cloud, tiny ball, whatever," said Giuliano. "Same size, done by dinner."

Muhammad didn't sit down. He flipped through the science book on the shelf until he found the table of particle masses, and then he read the number twice because it seemed ridiculous. "Guys. A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron." Giuliano dropped a marble. "One thousand eight hundred thirty-six? That's not a science number, that's a gym score." "It's real," Muhammad said, tapping the page. "So almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus. If we use the same size ball for both, the model is basically a lie with googly eyes." Sehaj held up a peppercorn beside a marble. "So, marbles for protons and neutrons, and these specks for electrons?"

They rebuilt the whole thing on a wire hanger. Twelve marbles clustered in the middle, six peppercorns dangling on long loops of fishing line, so far out the atom took up half the garage. Muhammad taped a label that read DO NOT JUDGE MY ELECTRONS BY THEIR SIZE. Giuliano decided the finished model should hang from the ceiling, and he grabbed one of the fishing-line loops to lift it. There was a small snap, the line gave way, and the nucleus plunged down and cracked an old flowerpot in the corner. Giuliano stared at the fracture running through the pottery. "Okay," he said slowly. "I believe the number now. I believed it with my foot."

Then Sehaj started laughing so hard she had to sit on a paint can. She pointed at the fallen nucleus, where one marble looked shinier than the rest, and Muhammad picked it up and turned it over. Scratched on the bottom in tiny letters were the words EASTER EGG, LOVE DAD. His father, who was renovating the garage next door and had been sneaking in all week, had secretly swapped one of the marble neutrons for a chrome ball bearing. "So our atom has one impostor," Muhammad said, grinning. He set the shiny marble on the workbench, then found a bottle labeled CORROSIVE in the corner cupboard and moved it far away from the peppercorns. "New rule," he announced. "Nobody touches the electrons but me." Giuliano raised his hand anyway and asked, "Can I at least be the one who drops the nucleus next time?"

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Carson had forty-one dollars and one crumpled coupon in his pocket, and he needed sixty more for the green sneakers in the window of Sole City. The mannequin in the display wore a sign that said "EVERYONE'S WEARING THEM," and below it, in shiny letters, "The most legendary, unbeatable, must-have shoe of the year." Carson read the sign twice. Everyone was a big word. He had never once seen a kid at school in green sneakers.

Inside the mall food court, his friend Axelle was scrolling her phone between bites of pretzel. "Look," she said, turning the screen toward him. "Dwayne sent me this video. A famous basketball player says these are the greatest shoes he's ever laced up."

"Does he mean it?" Carson asked.

Axelle squinted at the tiny caption under the video. "It says #ad right here. And in the corner, 'Paid partnership.'" She tapped the screen. "My brother told me that in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission makes influencers and celebrities clearly say when they got paid or got free stuff to promote something."

"So the player didn't just buy them because he loved them," Carson said slowly. "Somebody gave them to him, or paid him." That changed things. He looked at the video again, and now the player's grin looked more like a job than a feeling.

They walked back to Sole City together to think it over. The saleswoman said, "These are flying off the shelves. You'd better grab a pair before they're gone." Flying off the shelves, Carson thought. He could see the shelf. Twelve boxes sat there, neat and untouched, and a thin layer of dust sat on the top one. If they were really flying, wouldn't the shelf be emptier? He tested his idea by asking a simple question: "How many have you sold this week?" The saleswoman checked her tablet and admitted it was two.

"It's kind of the definition of irony," Axelle said outside the store. "The sign says everyone's wearing them, and nobody's even buying them here." Carson laughed. It also provoked something in him, a stubborn little itch to check before believing.

That night he sent Dwayne a message: "Did you know the basketball guy got paid? Look for #ad in the caption. It's the law. Want to come to the mall Saturday? I'm saving up, but I'm going to compare prices first."

Dwayne wrote back in eleven seconds: "WHOa. I did NOT see the #ad. My mom says there's a shoe outlet two blocks past the mall with the same shoes for less. Saturday. Bring the coupon."

On Saturday, Carson counted his money on the outlet counter: sixty-eight dollars, plus the coupon. The cashier rang it up, dropped the shoes in a bag, and said, "Have a good one."

Carson held the bag over his head so Dwayne and Axelle could see it from the door. "Green," he called, "for thirty percent less than legendary."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A novel's theme is usually implied rather than stated outright, so readers infer it from what the characters do and what happens to them.
story:
Isabelle sat at the kitchen table with her library copy of "The Trail to Blue Lake" open in front of her, a sticky note in her hand. The assignment from Ms. Petrov said: identify the theme, then back it up with a quotation from the text. Isabelle had assumed this would be easy. Somewhere in the book, surely, there was a sentence that said the moral, and all she had to do was find it, underline it, and copy it onto her homework sheet.

She flipped pages. The main character, a boy named Russ, got lost, shared his food with a stranger, lied about being brave, and finally admitted he was scared. Isabelle hunted for a line like "The lesson of this story is..." Nothing. She checked the last chapter twice, thinking morals might coincide with endings, the way the best part of a movie sometimes does. Still nothing. "This book forgot its own lesson," she muttered.

Her little brother wandered in and stole a cracker off her plate. "What are you doing?" he asked. "Looking for a sentence that doesn't exist," she said. He nodded as if this were a normal household activity and left.

She tried a different idea, a detective idea. What if the book never said the theme out loud? What if she had to figure it out from what Russ did, like guessing a rule by watching what happened every time someone broke it? She made a category on her paper: Things Russ Did. Helped the stranger. Got helped back. Lied, and it went badly. Told the truth, and it went better. A pattern was forming, quiet as footprints.

For the quotation, she copied the moment Russ said, "I was scared the whole time, and I kept walking anyway." She wrote her theme above it and stared at the page. Then she texted her classmate Blake: did you find the sentence that states the moral? His reply came fast: "There isn't one. It's like the book is too polite to say it." Isabelle laughed and wrote her final answer.

The next day Ms. Petrov read Isabelle's paper, then read it again, and drew a small star in the corner. "How did you land on this?" she asked. Isabelle shrugged. "I searched everywhere first. Then I stopped looking for the answer and started looking at what everyone did." Ms. Petrov tapped the quotation. "Russ kept walking," she said. Isabelle grinned. "Exactly. Scared the whole time. Walking anyway."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Harper sat cross-legged on her bed with the laptop open and a list of names beside her: twenty-six classmates, one birthday party. The plan felt exceptional until she reached the email screen. If she pasted every address into the To line, then everyone would see everyone else's address, and Margaret had once spent a week untangling a flood of messages after hers got passed around. Was there some way to send one message that kept the addresses hidden? She stared at the three empty boxes, To and CC and BCC, and wondered what the letters even meant.

She tried an experiment. She typed a test message to her own address in the To line, added her dad's address in the BCC line, and hit send. Then she walked to the kitchen where her dad was making sandwiches and asked him to open the message and read her the names he could see at the top. "Just yours," he said, chewing. "There's nobody else listed." Harper inhaled so fast she nearly choked on nothing. So BCC was the hiding place. The message reached her dad, but the To line never showed his address to anyone. She went back and typed it into the search bar anyway, just to check the words: blind carbon copy. People added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses. That was the mechanism, and it was exactly what she needed.

She built the real invitation carefully. Her own address went in To, all twenty-six classmates went into BCC, and then she wrote the message itself.

Hi everyone! My birthday party is Saturday at 2 at my house. There will be pizza and a tournament of the world's most ridiculous relay games. My address is on the paper flyer Ms. Tanaka has, since she said not to put home addresses in emails. Reply only to me, please. Harper.

When the replies came in that evening, she scrolled through them hunting for proof. Archer wrote, "Can Margaret be on my relay team?" Margaret wrote, "I'm bringing the noise makers." Nobody's address appeared anywhere except her own, and no accidental Reply All had spilled the whole class list into view. She copied the To and BCC lines into her notebook and drew a box around BCC, like a little room where addresses could stand without being seen.

At school on Monday, Archer slid into the seat beside her. "How'd you invite the whole class without showing everybody's addresses?" he asked. "BCC," Harper said. "Blind carbon copy." Archer leaned over her notebook and tapped the box she had drawn. "Show me where that button lives," he said, pulling the classroom laptop toward them.

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: The Python programming language is named after the BBC comedy show Monty Python's Flying Circus, not after the snake.
story:
Camille typed her loop for the third time and pressed Enter. Instead of the times table for 7, the screen filled with lines like 7 times 1 equals 7111111111111, as if her program had gone rebellious and refused to follow instructions. "Why is it gluing the numbers together?" she muttered. On the next computer, Iris was drawing a snake coiled around the words PYTHON CLUB, its tongue flicking at the letter P.

"Ms. Vargas says our logo should be funny, not scary," Iris said, frowning at her drawing. "But how do I make a snake funny?"

Camille leaned over. Something was tickling the back of her mind, a fact she'd read once and half forgotten. Could the name really not be about the snake at all? She pulled up the search page and typed "why is Python called Python." The answer made her laugh out loud. "Iris. It's named after Monty Python's Flying Circus. The comedy show. Not the snake."

Iris stared at her. "So my snake is wrong? Completely wrong?"

"Totally wrong. It should be, like, a giant foot stomping down, or a parrot." Camille was already sketching possibilities in the margin of her notebook while her program waited on the screen.

Then she stopped laughing and looked back at her error. The numbers were gluing together because she'd never told the program that the user's answer was a number; the computer thought it was text, and text just sticks side by side. Was that it? An idea germinated in her head, small but definite. She added one word, int, around the input, and ran it again. The screen printed a clean column, 7 times 1 equals 7, all the way to 7 times 12 equals 84.

"Look at that," she said. "One little word."

Iris held up a fresh drawing, a parrot wearing a tiny graduation cap. "Dead parrot sketch," she said. "Ms. Vargas is going to love it."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground, like granite, has large crystals, while rock that cools fast at the surface, like basalt, has tiny ones.
story:
Bennett knelt on the gravel bar where the trail crossed the creek and turned over a dark pebble. Steven crouched beside him, holding his own rock like a prize. Mr. Zhu had said whoever sorted the most rocks correctly into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic before lunch would get to pick the snack spot on the way home, and Steven wanted that spot so badly he had already claimed it twice.

"Dark and plain, no sparkles," Bennett said. "Igneous. Basalt, probably."

"Mine's got sparkles all over," Steven said, holding out a pale chunk with glittering flecks. "Granite. Also igneous, but way better. Igneous means it was melted once."

Shyla sat on a log, sorting sedimentary rocks by their stripes, like layers in a sandwich. "You two are just guessing."

"I'm not guessing. I made a rule." Bennett lined up his finds. "If it sparkles with big chunks, like the granite countertop in my kitchen, it cooled slowly underground. If it's dark and the crystals are so tiny you can't see them, it cooled fast at the surface, like basalt." He held up the dark pebble. "This one came out fast."

"So it's an algorithm," Shyla said, coming over to look. "Sparkly and pale, slow. Dark and dull, fast. Then the layers go to sedimentary, and anything wavy or squeezed is metamorphic."

"It's not an algorithm, it's just a rule," Steven said, but he was already checking his pile. He picked up a dark rock he had labeled granite and squinted at it, then moved it to the basalt side without a word.

At the trailhead, Mr. Zhu went through the bags one at a time, like a judge opening anonymous contest entries so nobody could be graded on faces, only on rocks. Bennett got eleven right. Steven got eleven right too, and Shyla got twelve.

"Guess we both pick the snack spot," Bennett said.

Steven held up his granite chunk, turning it so the big crystals caught the sun. "Fine. But I'm showing the cashier my rock when we pay."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Choral music is often written for four voice parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass, from highest to lowest.
story:
Elizabeth stood in the kitchen with the choir handout spread on the counter. Ms. Levy had said everyone had to pick a part before Tuesday's rehearsal, and Elizabeth had circled soprano, because that was the part she had heard on the recording. Now she was not so sure.

She hummed the top line of "Down by the Riverside" while she waited for the kettle. It sat comfortably in her voice, like a shelf at the right height. Then she hummed the lower line, the one Makayla liked, and it sat lower, snugger, in a spot she had to reach for.

Her mother put down her mug. "What are you doing?"

"Testing something. The choir is in four parts. Soprano, alto, tenor and bass, highest to lowest. Makayla says altos hold the harmony against the sopranos, and I want to try that." Elizabeth hummed both lines at once, one after the other, then tried to sing the lower one while the recording on her tablet sang the higher one. The first time, her voice slid upward and followed the melody like a dog following a scent. She stopped the recording.

She tried again, pressing one earphone to her ear so the soprano line came in loud and close. She planted her feet, thought of the lower note as a floor she could stand on, and sang. The two lines leaned against each other. When she finished, her throat felt warm, the way her hands did after carrying grocery bags up the stairs.

At school on Monday, Aditya asked which category she had chosen. "Soprano," Elizabeth said. "I changed my mind back. Alto is harder, but soprano is where my voice actually lives. The fundamental thing I learned is that harmony isn't about picking the best part. It's about holding your line while someone else holds theirs."

Aditya grinned. "Okay. But if you drift into my part on Tuesday, I'm elbowing you."

"Fair," said Elizabeth, and she hummed her line all the way down the hall.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Closing a switch completes the circuit so current flows; opening it makes a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once.
story:
David had one job in the science fair project: build the circuit for the model house, with a battery, a switch, and a bulb, and be able to explain why it lit. Anaya had made the house out of cardboard, complete with tiny curtains, and Alexa had painted it. If David's circuit failed in front of Ms. Santos-Reyes tomorrow, the whole grade would see a dark little house sitting on the table.

He tested it that afternoon in the classroom while Anaya held the flashlight. He flipped the switch down. Nothing. He flipped it up. Nothing. The bulb stayed dark.

"Maybe the battery's dead," Anaya said.

"It's brand new," David said. He thought about what a circuit actually was, a loop, invisible current going around it like runners on a track. If there was a gap anywhere in the loop, the runners would stop. The switch couldn't make a gap in only one spot; opening it stopped everything in the loop at once. So a dark bulb meant a gap somewhere, maybe somewhere he hadn't even touched. He followed every wire with his finger, slow, careful, while Anaya leaned in so close her braid almost touched the table. At the back corner, one wire had slipped loose from its clip, hidden behind the cardboard wall where nobody would ever look.

He clipped it back on. Flipped the switch down, and the bulb glowed. Flipped it up, and the light died instantly.

"When the switch closes, it completes the circuit so current flows," David said, practicing. "When it opens, there's a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once."

At the fair, Ms. Santos-Reyes bent toward the little house, and David felt his stomach tighten. She studied it, then flipped the switch herself. The bulb lit under the tiny curtains. "Impressive," she said. "Though I have to ask, who was your tutor on this? It's very polished work."

"It's legitimate," David said. "I built it. Found a loose wire behind the wall and everything." Ms. Santos-Reyes picked up the house, turned it over, and laughed. "Then you should know," she said, "that this bulb only lights because you're holding the switch down with your thumb."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Michael sat cross-legged on Gregoire's bedroom floor with Gregoire's phone in his lap, watching the group chat scroll. The project for Ms. Hoffmann's class was due at eight o'clock tonight, and the three of them, Michael, Gregoire, and Eshal, were supposed to be building a poster about ancient Egypt together. Eshal's messages kept appearing, one after another, full of ideas about the pharaohs and a section on the Twelfth Dynasty, which she insisted was the most interesting one. Michael envied how fast her thoughts arrived, tidy and complete, while his own were still tangled up somewhere between the pyramids and the Nile.

But Eshal had stopped answering twenty minutes ago. The last thing she had sent was "I found a great fact about the Twelfth Dynasty" and then nothing. Gregoire was downstairs getting snacks, so Michael typed the only thing he could think of: "WHERE ARE YOU." He pressed send before he really looked at it. The letters sat on the screen, big and pale against the grey bubble, and they seemed louder than any of the other messages, the way a shout in a quiet library seems louder than a shout at a football game.

Eshal replied almost instantly. "why are you yelling?"

Michael stared at the words. He had not been yelling. He had been whispering, actually, because Gregoire's little sister was napping down the hall. He typed back, "i wasn't yelling," and then deleted it, because arguing would waste time they did not have. In this room, with the door shut and the rain ticking against the window, he had written a message meant for just one person, but it had gone out into the chat where anyone could read it, and somehow the big letters had turned his quiet question into something that felt like a scolding. He thought about how his mom wrote whole emails in capitals when she was in a hurry, and how he had always pictured her practically shouting at her sister through the screen.

He tried an experiment. He typed the same words again, small letters only: "where are you." It looked softer on the screen, like a tap on the shoulder instead of a knock on a door. He sent it and waited, his thumb hovering.

Eshal answered right away. "sorry, phone died. i was charging it. i have the dynasty facts, send me what you two wrote." Gregoire came back up with a bowl of pretzels and read over Michael's shoulder. "You yelled at her," he said, grinning. "It was an accident," Michael said. "From now on I'm keeping my letters quiet and rebellious-free."

They finished the poster sections in time, and Eshal sent a photo of her neat handwriting for the timeline. At 7:52, Michael attached everything and sent it to Ms. Hoffmann, then flopped back against Gregoire's bed. His phone buzzed one last time. "good work, team," Eshal wrote, all in small letters, calm as anything.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
The group chat revolved around one topic all Saturday morning: SlideBook, the app everyone in seventh grade had apparently joined overnight. Gordon had posted eleven screenshots of his dog wearing virtual sunglasses. Deborah had posted a single message that said only "meet me here at 7?" with a link. Lily sat cross-legged on her bed with her dad's old phone and tapped Sign Up.

The first box asked for her birthday. She typed it honestly, and a red line appeared at the bottom of the screen. Users must be 13 or older to create an account. She frowned at it, deleted the year, and tried again with a year that made her fourteen. The red line vanished, but her thumb hovered. Her plan felt aggressive for something so small, like throwing a snowball at a locked door. She put the phone down and typed in the chat instead.

"why does it keep asking my birthday," she wrote.

"mine did that too," Deborah replied. "i just changed the year."

"that's what i was gonna do but it felt weird that they care so much"

Gordon sent three thinking-face emojis, then a voice message. "My cousin says it's a law or something. For kids under 13, websites have to get your parents to say yes before they can collect your info. Some privacy act from 1998. That's why everything says you have to be 13."

Lily played the message twice. She looked at the window, where her neighbor Ms. Singh was stappling gray insulation panels along her garage wall, sealing out the cold for winter. Everything private needed some kind of barrier, she thought, even information.

She typed, "so if i lie about my age, they collect my stuff without my mom knowing, and that's exactly what the law says they can't do unless she says ok." Then she opened a new message, to her mom this time, not the group. "Can I ask you something about SlideBook?"

In the kitchen her mom read the sign-up screen, checked a box marked parental consent, and filled in her own email while the pasta water heated up. "You could have just changed the year," she said.

"I know. Gordon's cousin said some people do."

Back upstairs, Deborah had sent six messages asking whether Lily was coming to the virtual meet-up at seven. Lily created her account, real birthday and all, and posted a screenshot of her new profile. Deborah answered fast: "finally!! i've been waiting forever." Lily added a smiley, set her profile to private so only friends could see it, and started typing a reply to Gordon's dog.

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned, from lowest to highest, to G, D, A and E, with each string a musical fifth above the one before.
story:
Mr. Schneider's garage smelled like sawdust and old coffee. He set a violin on the workbench between a bucket of paintbrushes and a plastic vessel full of screws, and Caleb picked the violin up like it might be toxic.

"Four strings," said Mr. Schneider, tapping each one. "Lowest to highest, G, D, A, E. Each one's a fifth above the string before it." He plucked the A string, then turned on a small metal box that hummed the same note. "Tune the others off that one. I'll be inside. Don't touch the table saw." He left before Caleb could justify why he would ever touch a table saw.

Caleb plucked the A until it matched the box. Easy. Then he plucked the D below it and it sounded like a cat complaining. He remembered the order: G, D, A, E, fifths going up. So D was a fifth below A. He tightened the peg a little, plucked, tightened again. Now the two strings rang together in a smooth, hollow sound he could feel in his teeth.

Jackson stuck his head in through the side door. "Is that a violin? I thought you were doing guitar."

"It's whatever sounds good by Friday," Caleb said. "Mr. Schneider's teaching me for the talent show." He plucked the G string and turned its peg, and the whole garage seemed to wobble. "Whoa. Too far." He backed it off, plucked, listened, and the wobble shrank to a shimmer.

The E string fought him for a whole minute, going from screech to almost-there to screech again, while Jackson held the humming box closer like a priest with incense. Then Caleb turned the peg a hair, plucked both E and A together, and the shimmer vanished into one clean, ringing sound.

"Play something," Jackson said.

Caleb dragged the bow across all four strings at once. Jackson fell backwards into a shelf of empty paint cans, and from the kitchen window Mr. Schneider shouted, "That's not tuning, that's an alarm!"

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
story:
Aria sat cross-legged in front of the family computer, her science fair notebook open on the desk beside the keyboard. At the top of the page she had written "Which hot chocolate tastes best: name brand or store brand?" and under it, her plan so far. It was not much of a plan. Her little brother's spelling quiz results, condense on her water glass, the tabs for her history homework on the fall of an absolute monarchy, nothing helped.

She typed "how do scientists test if a medicine works" into the search bar, because Mr. Nwosu had said her project should work like a real experiment. The first good result described a double-blind trial. Aria read the sentence twice, then a third time. In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results. She leaned back. If a scientist serving the pills could accidentally tip people off just by acting hopeful, then she could do the same thing with hot chocolate, handing someone a cup and saying "try this one, it's the good one."

She grabbed the phone and called Hillary. "Come over Saturday. I need you for my experiment."

"Is this more of your rebellious anti-name-brand campaign?" Hillary asked. "Because I already signed your petition."

"It's science. Listen. You can't know which cup is which when you hand them to people."

There was a pause on the line. "Wait, I don't even get to know?"

"Neither do I, and neither do the tasters. Dallas can put the samples in identical cups and label them A and B somewhere I can't see, then leave the room while you serve them."

Saturday morning, Dallas arrived with two boxes of hot chocolate and a face that said she could not believe she'd given up her weekend for this. Aria made her the "sample master" and sent her into the kitchen with instructions to mix both kinds, label the cups, and keep the answer sheet sealed in an envelope. Dallas emerged looking pleased with her power. "I am the monarchy of this kitchen," she announced, "and I rule in secret."

"You're a sample master," Aria said. "That's not the same thing."

Hillary served the cups without a word, keeping her face blank even when Dallas hummed suspiciously near cup B. Six tasters came and went, including Mr. Nwosu from next door, who wrote his ranking in careful pencil. When Aria opened the envelope, store brand had won, five votes to one.

"I really thought the name brand would win," Hillary said, staring at the tally. "I probably would have handed those cups out differently."

"That's the whole point," Aria said. She copied the results into her notebook and underlined them twice.

From the kitchen, Dallas called out, "Round two, anybody? The queen demands more data."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
Bentley lay wedged into the corner of the living room couch with a box of tissues, his third cold since fall, and he was mad about it. "Three," he muttered into the ceiling. "Three colds and it's barely February. Something's wrong with me."

The doorbell rang, and Ezra came in carrying Bentley's homework folder and his own phone. "Ms. Brown says get better, and also we have a quiz Thursday, but she'll postpone it if the whole class votes for Friday." He dropped onto the far cushion. "You look like a potato."

"Thanks." Bentley pulled the blanket higher. "I've been thinking. Three colds since fall. My dad had one. One. Am I broken?"

Ezra shrugged, so Bentley grabbed his own tablet from the coffee table and typed. He read, stopped, and read again. "Okay. According to the CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year. And kids often catch more than that."

"More than adults? Really?"

"That's what it says." Bentley sat up, which made his head complain, and kept going anyway. "So I'm not broken. I'm just eleven." He decided to test it. "Get the class chat up. Ask everybody how many colds they've had since September."

Ezra sent the message, and answers stacked up fast. Kaelyn: two. A boy down the street: four and a half, because he counted a day and a half of sore throat. Ezra himself: two. Out of nineteen replies, almost nobody had fewer than two, and a bunch had three or more.

"So the pattern's real," Bentley said, writing tally marks on a napkin. "Everybody's gross, not just me." He grinned, then coughed. "Tomorrow you ask your dad how many he's had. If it's three or less, my theory holds, and that part is crucial."

Ezra pocketed the phone. "Your whole science project is a napkin of tally marks about boogers."

"My whole science project is data," Bentley said, and blew his nose like a trumpet.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Reframing means restating an insult in neutral words, turning "She's so selfish" into "You want a fairer share," so the conversation can keep moving.
story:
The argument had already started when Hannah reached the swings. Clarissa stood with her arms crossed by the climbing frame while Joshua sat on the top of the slide, glaring at the wood chips below. "She's so selfish," Clarissa said, loud enough for the whole playground to hear. "She hogs the good swing every single day and she never lets anyone else have a turn." Joshua slid down without looking at her. "You just call everything selfish when you don't get your way."

Hannah's stomach tightened. She had promised herself she would stay neutral this time. Last month, when the two of them had fought about a group project, she had taken Clarissa's side, and Joshua had refused to speak to her for a week. That was the moment she remembered now, standing between the swing set and the slide: him walking off across the field, his backpack bouncing, while she called his name and he never turned around. She had decided then that she would learn how to be a real mediator, the way her aunt did at work before she retired and moved to her small pension flat by the sea. Her aunt had shown her a book about it, and one page was folded over.

"Wait," Hannah said, stepping onto the wood chips between them. "Before anyone says anything else to each other, talk to me. Separately." She walked Clarissa over to the bench by the fence, out of Joshua's hearing. "Tell me what happened, but leave out the name-calling." Clarissa opened her mouth, probably to repeat "selfish," and Hannah held up a hand. "Here's the trick I read about. Reframing means restating an insult in neutral words." She paused. "So instead of 'she's so selfish,' try 'I want a fairer share of the good swings.' Say it that way and I can pass it on without starting a war." Clarissa blinked, then laughed a short, surprised laugh. "Fine. I want a fairer share. There. Happy?"

Hannah carried the message to the slide, then brought Joshua's answer back, which was that he felt blamed for things that felt random to him, since he took turns whenever anyone actually asked. She kept her face even both times, like carrying water in a cup without spilling. Back and forth she went, twice, three times, while a pair of sparrows invaded the space under the bench to hunt for dropped crumbs. On the fourth trip the words changed. Clarissa said, "So he didn't know I was waiting?" and Joshua said, "So she wasn't trying to grab everything?" They looked at each other across the wood chips.

Joshua climbed off the slide and walked over. "You could have just told me you wanted the swing after me," he said. Clarissa shrugged. "You could have just asked if I was waiting." Neither of them apologized, exactly, but Joshua offered her the good swing first tomorrow, and she said she would time him today so it felt even. They wandered off toward the monkey bars together, arguing mildly about who was faster.

Hannah sat down on the bench and let out a slow breath. Her aunt's folded page had worked, and she had not taken a side once. She watched the sparrows scatter as the two of them ran past, chasing each other toward the far end of the playground.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, to pinpoint an exact spot.
story:
Stella spread the map of Portugal across the library table so flat that the corners stopped curling. Miley leaned over her shoulder, and Manreet pulled up a chair on the other side. Their geography project was due Thursday, and the assignment said they had to give the location of Lisbon using latitude and longitude, not just "it's on the coast, next to the ocean." Ms. Menon had already brought them an atlas from the reference shelf, and now the three of them were stuck on the same line: 38° 43' N.

"Forty-three minutes," Stella said slowly. "Why minutes? Is the map telling us what time it is there?"

"Maybe the measurements were taken at a certain time of day," Miley offered. Manreet frowned at the tiny mark between the numbers, which looked a bit like an apostrophe.

Stella ran her finger down the edge of the map and noticed something. The space between 38° and 39° was divided into small tick marks, sixty of them, and halfway down the row a label read 30'. So whatever a minute was, it lived inside a degree. She began to hypothesize: if degrees were split into sixty parts, then a minute had to be one of those parts, a fraction of distance, not a sliver of time. She tested the idea by counting the ticks from 38° to the 43' mark. Exactly forty-three small marks.

"So each degree of latitude is divided into sixty minutes," she said, tapping the edge, "and it's not about clocks at all."

Manreet was already flipping the page to the index. "It says here each minute is divided into sixty seconds, too. Like sixty tiny steps inside each minute, to pinpoint an exact spot."

"That's why it's so precise," Miley said. "We could find the exact square the library stands on."

They hunted through the atlas until they found a detailed city map of Lisbon, with its tiled squares and its old artisan quarter, where the streets were named for the craftsmen who once worked there. Stella copied the coordinates onto her notepad, then added the seconds from the small inset box, careful with every number.

Ms. Menon paused at their table on her way past, saw the notepad, and smiled at the neat string of degrees, minutes, and seconds. Stella slid the map toward her and pointed at the mark they had found, sixty-one tick marks in from the corner, exactly where they had calculated it would be.

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: Ships measure water depth with sonar: they send a pulse of sound down and time how long its echo takes to return from the seabed.
story:
Luca stood in his grandfather's garage beside a steel washtub full of water, holding a wrench. Marie and Arnaud sat on an overturned crate, waiting, because Luca had promised them a demonstration and they had heard promises before. "Sound travels faster through water than air," he said. "You can't see that, so we're going to hear it instead."

He tapped the wrench against the rim. A thin ping rang out through the air, and a moment later a second, duller sound came back from the far wall. "Echo," said Arnaud. "Big deal." That was when Luca told them about the museum trip last spring, the day his whole class had crowded around a tank with a plastic lake in it. At the exhibit you pressed a button to send a pulse of sound down through the water, and a screen timed how long the echo took to come back up from the bottom, from the lakebed. Marie frowned. "So?" "So that's how ships measure water depth," Luca said. "It's called sonar. They send one pulse down and time the echo from the seabed. At the museum the echo came back fast, way faster than our wall echo, and the lake wasn't even deep."

He crouched by the washtub and tapped the wrench on a bolt he had dropped into the water, so the sound had to travel down and back up. Marie leaned in. Arnaud held his phone like a stopwatch. They counted, and the answer came out shorter than the air echo across the same distance. Arnaud was still arguing that he'd clicked too late when Ms. Navarro, the neighbour, pushed open the side door with a bag of tomatoes.

"That racket," she said. "The tapping." She pointed at the workbench, where the old air compressor sat with its motor ticking, its piston sliding up and down inside the cylinder, humming a note that had saturated the whole garage since they started. Luca realized they hadn't been timing his wrench at all. "Arnaud," he said, "we're doing it again. This time I unplug it first."

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: The Moon rises on average about 50 minutes later each day, because it moves along its orbit while Earth turns.
story:
Ava had been standing outside the science museum for exactly forty minutes, and the Moon had not risen. Yesterday it had popped over the roofline at 6:20, right when she and Kaylie were leaving the planetarium, and she had promised Gerald she would show him tonight. Gerald had come. The Moon had not.

"It's cloudy," Gerald said, squinting at a sky that was perfectly clear.

"Maybe it's shy," said Kaylie, who was eating fries she had clearly inherited from her brother, since she kept saying they were his and he wouldn't miss them.

Ava checked her watch. 6:55. Yesterday, 6:20. She did the subtraction twice, because it seemed rude. "It's late," she said. "By, like, fifty minutes."

"Moons aren't late," Gerald said. "That's not a thing that happens."

Inside, the museum was doing a voluntary moon lab, which meant you could skip it if you wanted, but nobody wanted to, because Mr. Korhonen had set up a lamp in the middle of a table and handed out Styrofoam balls on sticks. Ava took one and stuck a pencil through it, which felt like plumbing for planets, all pipes and fittings. The lamp was the Sun. The ball was the Moon. Her own head, Mr. Korhonen said, was Earth, and she should not take this personally.

She walked her Moon-ball around her head, watching the shadow slide across it. Half lit, then a crescent, then dark, then full again. That part she had more or less known. What she kept thinking about was the ball moving, orbit by orbit, while her head turned too. Yesterday's moonrise spot, the roofline, and today's. There had to be a reason the Moon showed up fifty minutes later tonight.

She walked the ball halfway around the lamp and kept going, and the roofline outside suddenly made a kind of sense she couldn't quite say out loud yet. She tried anyway, to Gerald, holding the ball at arm's length and turning slowly in a circle, like a person practicing an odd voluntary dance.

"So it's not late," she said. "It rises fifty minutes later every day, on average. It just moves while we spin. Yesterday I was mad at it and today I feel like it's doing exactly what it's supposed to do."

Gerald watched the ball go around her head one more time. "So tomorrow," he said, "we come at 7:45."

"Bring fries," said Kaylie.

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In The Hunger Games, mockingjays were never planned by the Capitol: they came from its engineered jabberjay birds breeding with wild female mockingbirds.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like burnt coffee, and Eli spread his copy of The Hunger Games across the table next to the plate of cookies. "Okay," he said. "Every time the mockingjay shows up, I'm writing down what it means. That's my project." Jaiden pulled out his own book, and Neil dropped into the chair across from them, already chewing a cookie.

"Good luck," Jaiden said. "The bird means something different every chapter. In the beginning it's just a pin. Then it's District Twelve. Then it's Katniss herself." Eli drew three columns: chapter, what the bird does, what people say about it. He had decided to invest the whole weekend in the chart, mostly because he'd argued with Jaiden about it on Friday and lost. He wanted evidence this time, not just a feeling.

Neil flipped to the back of his book and stopped. "Wait. Listen to this." He read out loud that mockingjays were never planned by the Capitol, that they came from its engineered jabberjay birds breeding with wild female mockingbirds. Jaiden sat up straight. "See? That's my point. The bird already means something before Katniss ever wears it. It means the Capitol messed up. It's a walking mistake."

Eli stared at his chart. His three columns suddenly felt too small. He drew a fourth column at the far left and labeled it what the Capitol wanted. Then he filled it in: jabberjays, planned. Mockingjays, not planned. The pin, not planned by Katniss either, just given to her. "It's like an equation," he said slowly. "The bird's meaning equals whatever the Capitol couldn't control." Jaiden leaned over to look, and for once he didn't argue.

Grandpa shuffled in, saw the papers, and grinned. "Mockingjays. I had this same fight in 2010." He went to the shelf and pulled down a battered copy, its margins crowded with blue ink. He dropped it on the table beside Eli's chart, and Eli opened it to the first chapter, where a note in faded handwriting read: "She doesn't choose the pin. The pin chooses her."

"Do you still believe that?" Eli asked.

Grandpa tapped the page twice. "Ask me after chapter ten."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The message appeared in the group chat at 7:04 on Tuesday evening: "Connor, that video of you rapping about the water cycle is still on the school website. My cousin in Ohio found it." Connor stared at his phone. He had posted the video three weeks ago, back when he thought he was funny, and he had deleted it two days later after Melody said, kindly but honestly, that it made her ears hurt. He typed back, "Impossible. I deleted it." Crystal answered with a link. It was the Ridgeview Middle School news page, and there he was, huge and immortal, rapping about evaporation in his dad's oversized sunglasses.

His thumbs hovered over the keyboard. He remembered the day he deleted it, how relieved he felt, how he'd imagined the video vanishing like a whiteboard erased at the end of class. Melody had missed that whole week anyway because of her concussion from the soccer game, so she'd never even seen the original. "How is it still there," he wrote, and then, deciding that didn't sound calm enough, "I mean, how can that be?" Crystal replied, "My cousin says he found it on the Wayback Machine. It's saved more than one trillion web pages, so stuff deleted from a public site can sometimes still be found."

Connor put the phone down on his desk and looked at it for a long moment. The Wayback Machine. He'd never heard of it. He thought of all the times his mom had said, careful, that's going on your permanent record, and he had assumed she meant a file in a filing cabinet somewhere. Now he understood that the permanent record was a robot that copied pages, trillions of them, and kept the copies even when the originals disappeared.

He typed carefully this time. "Can you ask your cousin to check if my post is in there too? The one about Mr. Levy's tie being affluent?" Crystal sent back a crying-laughing face, then: "You called his tie affluent? It means rich-looking." Connor winced. He had meant fancy, and instead he'd written a word he only half knew, on a public page, where a robot had probably photographed it forever. Then came a longer message: "Actually, don't bother him. I'll show you tomorrow at the library. I want to learn how it works anyway, because I correspond with a pen pal in Japan and she asked me if old websites can come back. Now I can tell her yes."

The next afternoon Crystal pulled up the archived school page, and there was Connor's tie post, frozen and slightly crooked on the screen, the way old snapshots always look. He had come to the library planning to ask her how to bury it, but sitting there, he found himself laughing instead. "You know what," he said, "leave it. If a trillion pages are saved anyway, hiding one dumb sentence is like hiding one grain of sand on a beach." He screenshotted it and sent it to Melody, who still hadn't seen it, with the message: "New material for when your head is better." Crystal leaned over and clicked forward through the archive, one saved page at a time.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Piper sat cross-legged on the desk chair in Loralie's room, watching the cursor blink on the laptop screen. "Sarah-Maude just texted me 'enjoy the smoothie,'" Loralie said, holding up her phone. "I never told her I was at the mall. Never told her about the smoothie place either. How does she know?" Piper leaned in, because that question itched at her like a tag in a shirt collar. Somebody knew something they shouldn't know, and things like that didn't just happen. Something was causing it, and the cause was somewhere she couldn't see.

"Text her back and ask," Piper said. "Word for word." Loralie typed: How did you know which store I was in? The answer came in a screenshot. It was a map of the mall, with a little cartoon version of Loralie standing right on top of the smoothie shop. At the top it said her name and "2 minutes ago." Piper read it twice. "What app is that?" Loralie tapped the corner of the screen. "It's the Snap Map. It shows your real-time location to your friends on a map." She said it lightly, like it was nothing, but Piper kept staring at the little cartoon Loralie, frozen on the exact tile outside the smoothie shop where the real Loralie had stood twenty minutes ago.

Piper tested it. She pulled out her own phone, opened her settings, and found a switch called Ghost Mode, which was off. She turned it on, then walked to the kitchen and back, and asked Loralie to check the map. The cartoon Piper had vanished from view. "See?" Piper said. "It only shows where you are if that switch is off. It was on for you, so it was telling everybody." Loralie's face went stiff and brittle, the way it did before a hard piano recital, and Piper remembered: the recital was at six, and it was already five fifteen. "Turn it off for me," Loralie said, shoving the phone across the desk. "I don't want to hunt through menus with my hands shaking."

While Loralie pulled on her recital shoes, Piper hunted through the settings until the switch flipped to green. Then, out of curiosity, she checked one more thing. She scrolled back through the map and noticed that a photo Loralie had posted at the mall three days earlier still sat pinned at that spot, like a fossil, for anyone on her list to open. "These don't go away, either," Piper said quietly. "People can look at them later." Loralie stopped lacing her shoe and looked at the screen for a long moment, then took the phone and, with one careful thumb, deleted the post. "Okay," she said. "Now help me find my other shoe before my mom gets here."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
Ms. Pritchard wrote one question on the board before anyone had even sat down: "Can a right thing be wrong?" The class groaned, but Emma leaned forward, because she knew exactly which story was coming. Last spring, the science club had split in two, and the fight had never really ended. Rosemary had told Ms. Pritchard that the mold-culture jars had broken by accident, when really Emery had knocked them over horsing around and begged Rosemary to say nothing. Rosemary had covered for her. Half the club quit over it.

"Let's take the case fairly," Ms. Pritchard said. "Rosemary, remind us of the facts." Rosemary stood, chin up. "Emery knocked over the jars. She asked me not to tell. I didn't tell. Later I admitted it." She sat down fast. Emery, two rows over, stared at her desk.

Emma raised her hand. "Here's what I don't get. We all agree on every single fact. Emery broke the jars. Emery asked. Rosemary kept quiet, then confessed. Nobody disputes any of it. So why are we still arguing?"

"Because it's controversial," said a boy near the window. "Fairness says she should have told on day one. Loyalty says a friend doesn't rat out a friend."

Emma thought about the day it happened. She had been the one who found the shattered glass and the ruined organisms inside, weeks of careful growing gone slimy and dead. She remembered wanting to cry, and she remembered watching Rosemary's face and thinking, even then, that Rosemary looked more scared of losing Emery than of lying. Emma had quit the club that week. She'd told her mom it was boring. It wasn't.

"Let's test something," Emma said, standing up. "Rosemary, if you could go back, would you do it again?" Rosemary was quiet so long that the radiator clicked twice. "I'd tell Emery to confess herself," she said finally. "But if she wouldn't, I don't know. Probably I'd still keep quiet. She needed me." Emery's head came up. "You'd cover for me again? After I got you grounded for a month?" Rosemary shrugged. "You're my friend. That's just true."

"So it's not the facts," Emma said slowly. "It's what people care about most. Rosemary cares about loyalty, and the people who quit care about fairness, and both sides can look at the exact same event and come out in different places." She looked at Emery. "Which side are you on?" Emery chewed her lip. "I'm on whichever side means Rosemary doesn't quit the club too."

Ms. Pritchard wrote a second line under the first: "Same facts, different values." She capped her marker. "Talk amongst yourselves. Emma, Emery, Rosemary, you three are the case study." Emma carried her chair over to Emery's desk, and Rosemary dragged hers around too, the three of them making a tight little triangle near the window.

"Club meets Thursday," Emma said. "If we persevere, maybe we can grow a new batch of organisms before the spring fair." Emery smiled, and Rosemary kicked her gently under the desk.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
Sebastian slouched in the desk chair, staring at the school laptop while his little sister's music thumped through the wall. On the screen was the plant fertilizer he'd picked for the science fair, the bag that promised BIGGER TOMATOES, and below it a video titled "This Fertilizer Changed My Garden." In the video, a man held up a tomato the size of a softball and said he'd used the fertilizer on one plant and got the biggest harvest of his life.

Sebastian typed a note: Fertilizer works, man on video had huge tomato. He looked at it. Something about it bugged him, the way a single pebble bugs you inside your shoe. One man. One garden. What if that man just had good soil? What if his neighbor across the street grew softball tomatoes every year with no fertilizer at all?

His phone buzzed. Kason: "my brother says he's immune to mosquitoes. got bitten once all summer. I got bitten 30 times." Sebastian grinned and typed back, "or your brother just smells bad to mosquitoes." Then he stopped. Same problem. One person's summer, no comparison, nothing to check it against.

He scrolled back to the fertilizer page and found a small link to a university study. Two hundred plots of tomato plants, identical soil, identical water, identical sun. Half the plots got the fertilizer and half got none, and the researchers measured both groups. Sebastian sat up straight. That was the difference. The man in the video had told a story about his one garden, but the study had tested many gardens against gardens just like them, minus the fertilizer. He opened his project document and started a new note: "A control group gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested. So any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing." He read it twice, then changed his plan. He would grow his own.

The next morning his mom drove him to the hardware store, where the cashier helped him find two identical pots, two identical bags of soil, and two cherry tomato seedlings that looked like twins. At school, Ms. Sandhu approved his plan with a stamp and a smile, and Reese leaned over from the next desk.

"Two pots?" Reese whispered. "Why not just one with fertilizer?"

"Then it's just a story about one plant," Sebastian said. "I need the other pot so I can compare."

Reese wanted in. "Can I take the control one home? I never get to keep the plants, my mom says my room's too dark. I'll measure it every single day, I promise."

"Deal," Sebastian said. "Same water, same window, same everything. I'll text you the schedule."

For six weeks they traded measurements like baseball cards. Sebastian's fertilized plant climbed its stick like a conductor leading an orchestra, shoots reaching in every direction, but it flowered late. Reese's plain plant stayed shorter and then, in week five, burst out with tiny green tomatoes all at once. At the fair, the judge counted twenty-three fruits on Reese's pot and nine on Sebastian's. Under the fertilizer's own rules, it had failed the test.

Reese stood beside the losing pot, practically glowing. "So my plant beat the fancy one."

"You beat it," Sebastian said. He wasn't even upset. He arranged the two pots side by side on the table, red fruit next to green, and propped up his chart where everyone could see both columns.

Then he spotted Kason dragging his brother toward the display. "See?" Sebastian called. "This is how you test your mosquito thing. You'd need a whole crowd of you, all summer, same yard." Kason laughed, and his brother groaned like a man about to resign from the mosquito family altogether, but he stopped at the table anyway and picked up the magnifying card Sebastian held out to him.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: A curtain call is when performers return to the stage at the end of a show to be recognized by the audience, usually with a bow.
story:
Ryder had one line in the spring concert, and he had practiced it so many times that his little sister could say it too. The real problem was the ending. Ms. Dang had drilled the songs, the entrances, even where to stand, but nobody had said what to do when the applause started. At the last rehearsal, a rumor began to circulate backstage that the eighth graders had a special plan, but nobody would tell the fifth graders what it was.

On the night of the show, the community theater smelled like dust and old velvet. Ryder stood in the back row of the chorus, sweating under the lights, and delivered his line, "The river remembers everything," without his voice cracking, which felt significant. The audience clapped. And then everything stopped. The kids on stage just stood there, smiling frozen smiles, because nobody had ever told them what came next.

Ryder thought fast. Last month he had watched a traveling play at this same theater, and he remembered something odd that he had filed away without knowing why: at the end, the actors came back out from the wings, one at a time, and bowed while people cheered. They hadn't done it during the show, only after. From the audience's perspective, it must look strange to clap at a row of kids standing like fence posts. This was the thing itself, he realized. He leaned toward Kailey, who stood beside him with her hands still folded from the final note.

"Curtain call," he whispered. "Watch, we bow."

"We were never taught a bow," Kailey whispered back.

"Neither were they," Ryder said, and he bowed, low and fast. Deborah caught on and bowed too, and the wave spread down the line until every kid on stage was bent over, and the applause grew louder, warm as a blanket. From the wings, Ms. Dang waved her arms, nodding, her hands urging them deeper.

Afterward, in the lobby, Kailey elbowed him. "Where'd you learn that?"

"I didn't learn it anywhere," Ryder said. "I just remembered it." He looked back at the stage where the curtain was coming down. "Next year, we teach it to the little kids first."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
Marcus raised his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "I know who broke the vase," he announced, and half the class turned to stare at him.

The vase had shattered during recess on Tuesday, right beside the fish tank in Mr. Qureshi's room. Nobody had confessed. Now, on Friday, Mr. Qureshi had stacked four index cards on his desk and asked the class what they thought had happened. Izabella said she'd seen Lambert running near the fish tank that morning. Lambert insisted he was only chasing a paper airplane. Someone else claimed a janitor's cart bumped the shelf. And a fourth kid swore the vase was already cracked before recess even started.

"Four stories," said Mr. Qureshi, tapping the cards. "Yesterday at the senior centre, my friend showed us a film like this. It was from 1950, by Akira Kurosawa, and it was called Rashomon. It tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other." He set the cards face down. "Every witness believed they were telling the truth."

Marcus copied the name into his notebook. He remembered the shape of the vase, blue with gold fish on it, and he remembered that the pieces on the floor had been spread in a wide fan, not piled in one spot. A wide fan meant the vase had flown sideways, like it had been knocked, not dropped straight down. He devised a test. If he could figure out where someone would have to stand to knock the vase that direction, he could compare it with each story.

At lunch he borrowed the paper airplane Lambert had folded, taped a small weight to its nose, and asked Lambert to throw it again after school while Izabella watched from the door. The plane curved left and clipped the shelf exactly where a cart handle would have been. "So you were running past the cart," Marcus said, "and the cart did the knocking, and then the janitor blamed you because you were the thing he saw." Lambert's shoulders dropped an inch. "I got in trouble at my old school," he said quietly. "For stuff I didn't do."

Izabella pulled her chair over so Lambert didn't sit alone. Marcus had planned a whole sophisticated argument to present on Monday, with diagrams, but listening to Lambert he thought a shorter one might do. He used the back of his notebook instead, where he kept his sketches, and drew the flight path of the airplane in careful pencil. Then he wrote his plan with an economy of words, just four lines. "We're all witnesses," he told them. "The trick is, we're all honest, too." Izabella grinned and stole his pencil to add a fifth line. "Then let's go tell Mr. Qureshi," she said.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: If a price is held above the equilibrium price, sellers offer more than buyers want, and unsold goods pile up as a surplus.
story:
Gabriel stood at the kitchen counter on a sticky June morning, staring at three enormous jugs of strawberry lemonade that had not sold the day before. His stand had been perfect, or so he'd thought. He'd built the sign himself, made the letters perfectly perpendicular to the sign's edges so they'd look professional, and set the price at four dollars a cup because the strawberries had been expensive at the farmer's market. Harper had helped him squeeze lemons for two hours. Now the jugs sat in the fridge, and every cup he hadn't sold was money he'd spent and would never get back.

"Maybe we should just charge less," Harper said, arriving with more lemons in a plastic bag. "Dennis bought one cup yesterday and said nobody at the pool would pay four dollars when the gas station sells lemonade for a dollar."

Gabriel frowned. He remembered his mother buying strawberries in February, when the little plastic box had cost almost seven dollars, and the same box in June costing three. He'd asked her why once, and she'd shrugged and said something about how many strawberries exist in each season. He hadn't understood it then. Now he scrutinized the jugs, the price sign, the empty street outside, and something clicked.

"In winter, everybody wants strawberries and there aren't many, so the price goes up," he said slowly. "In summer, there are tons, so it goes down. And if you charge more than people will actually pay..." He pointed at the fridge. "You end up with that. Jugs and jugs nobody wants."

"Surplus," Harper said, grinning. "That's the word Mr. Desir used when he was grumbling about the book fair last year."

They rewrote the sign together, this time with the new price, one dollar fifty, crooked but readable. By four o'clock the jugs were empty, and Gabriel counted the money twice, feeling the weight of the coins in his palm. He still wasn't sure whether the February strawberries and his lemonade were really the same thing, or whether he'd just gotten lucky with the weather. Harper was already talking about next weekend and watermelons.

"One dollar a cup," Gabriel said, and flipped the sign face down against the table.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
