knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
Jade stood outside room 412 for a long time before she pushed the door open. Her grandmother had died two hours before dawn, and the machines were gone now, which somehow made the room feel louder instead of quieter. A nurse had mentioned that the backup generator would kick in if the storm outside cut the power, and Jade caught herself wondering about that, how a machine nobody ever saw could be waiting the whole time, ready. Maybe grief worked the same way, humming underneath everything, invisible until it wasn't.

Her father was on the phone with the rabbi, writing fast. Jade leaned over his notepad and saw the word shiva circled twice. Seven, he said when he hung up. It came from the Hebrew word for seven, and it meant seven days of mourning after the burial, seven days when visitors would come to the house to comfort them. "Starting tonight," he added, "right after we bury her. The burial has to happen before the storm gets worse."

That was the deadline, and it left Jade with a problem she couldn't stop chewing on. Ameera and Rylen had texted six times already, asking what to say, and Jade didn't know. What words covered a hole that size? She tried drafting something in her head, crossed it all out, and finally decided to run a test. She would tell them the truth: come anyway, say nothing if nothing came.

They arrived that evening with torn, rain-spotted notes they never unfolded. Rylen stood stiffly by the snack table. Ameera sat on the floor next to Jade and just stayed there, and Jade discovered something her scribbled speeches never could have demonstrated: the silence with a friend inside it was different from plain silence.

The twist came at the door. Grandma's oldest friend arrived, took one look at the crowded living room, and said, "Everyone here is being so careful with me, so impartial, like I might break." She laughed a wet laugh. "You children, you got it right without trying."

Jade looked at Ameera, still on the floor, still not saying anything, and patted the space beside her.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Raphael was sitting at the family computer with his poem assignment open on the screen when the message from Arielle popped up. She had sent a photo of her new rabbit, a gray ball of fluff sitting in a cardboard box, and underneath it she wrote that her poem was going to be about him for Mr. Henry's class. Raphael zoomed in on the rabbit, then, out of curiosity, right-clicked the image and chose "Get Info." He had learned that trick last week when he wanted to see how big a file was. A panel slid open with dates and camera settings, and at the bottom, a small map appeared with a pin on it. The pin sat on Maple Court, three streets over from school, exactly where Arielle lived. Next to the map were numbers, a latitude and longitude, pointing straight at her house. He sat back. He had never told Arielle where she lived, and she had never told him either, yet here was her street, written into the picture itself.

He remembered the word from a video he had watched about phones: hidden data written into a photo file. He thought the video had called it EXIF metadata, but he wanted to be sure it worked the way he thought. He took a photo of his own desk with his tablet, sent it to himself, and opened it on the computer. He right-clicked, chose "Get Info," and scrolled to the bottom. There was the map again, and this time the pin pointed at his own house, at the end of his own street, four houses from the corner. So that was it. When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into the hidden data in the file, and anyone who opens the details can see them.

Raphael looked at his poem, which was one stanza long and needed two more, but he typed a message to Arielle first. "Check the details of the rabbit photo," he wrote. "Right-click, then Get Info. Scroll down." While he waited, he turned off location services on his tablet, thinking it would also help conserve the battery. His answer arrived in pieces: "WHAT," then "that's my house," then "how." He wrote back that the hidden data in a photo file is called EXIF metadata, and that hers had her street written right into it. A minute later she sent a thumbs-up and said she had just turned her location off, and that she was only ever sending him rabbit pictures from now on anyway.

He went back to the poem, wrote a second stanza about the rabbit's ears, and decided the third one would be about the cardboard box, because a box was a better home than it looked. Before he closed his messages, Arielle sent one more line: "Shiloh posts ten pictures a day. Should we tell him?" Raphael looked at the photo of the gray rabbit still open on his screen, the map pin gone now that Arielle had fixed it, and started typing.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users.
story:
Sydney sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with her mother's old laptop, chewing the end of her pencil. Tomorrow morning her class was holding a debate, and Ms. Tesfaye had assigned her the opening statement. The question on the board had been: is it fair for an advertisement to disguise itself as a regular search result? Sydney had exactly one evening to build a case.

She typed "are ads fair" into the search bar and got back a mush of opinions, a quiz site, and something about fair trade chocolate. Annabella had told her after school that the trick was specific keywords, so Sydney tried again: "search engine paid results rules." That was better. She tried "paid results versus natural results" and got a page that looked promising.

Then she noticed something odd. The first link on the page had a tiny grey box beside it that said "Ad." The ones below it did not. Sydney had never really looked at that box before. She scrolled down, found another one, and counted three little boxes on the whole page. They were the same size as the other links, the same shade of blue. Only the small grey label made them different. She copied one of the ad links and one of the plain links into a document so she could show the class tomorrow.

Naila rang the doorbell at seven, holding a bag of pretzels and her own tablet. "I found something," Naila said, dropping onto the couch. "In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results have to be clearly distinguishable from natural results." She turned the tablet around. "Or they risk deceiving users. That's a quote."

Sydney felt the tight spot behind her ribs loosen. That was the rule, the whole reason the little grey boxes existed. "So the ads aren't supposed to hide," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "If you can't tell them apart, that counts as deceiving people." She looked back at her screen, at the three ads sitting quietly at the top of the results. Then she tried a small experiment. She typed the name of a popular game and searched it. The first four links all carried the grey "Ad" box, and beneath them came an ordinary fan site with none. The pattern held.

"Can I confide something?" Naila said, lowering her voice even though only the two of them were in the room. "I was hesitant to sign up for the debate team. I thought I'd freeze up in front of everyone." She pushed the pretzel bag toward Sydney. "But this is actually kind of fun."

Sydney took a handful and kept typing. She added a line about the Federal Trade Commission, then a line about her own grey-box count. By eight thirty she had a full page, and on it she had written her closing image: every result wearing its own honest little label, like name plates on the doors of a residence where you could always tell who actually lived there.

She read the last sentence out loud, then hit print and listened to the pages slide out into the tray.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, the same substance as a gas, so boiling is a physical change even though it makes bubbles.
story:
The pot had just started to rumble when Gavin set his notebook on the counter and wrote "bubbles = chemical change" in capital letters. He was so sure of it that he'd told Annie at school, and Annie had laughed at him for a whole lunch period. Now he had a plan. If bubbles meant a chemical change, then boiling water was producing something new, and he was going to catch it.

Mr. Qureshi from next door had lent him the thermometer from his garage. "You'll want to calibrate it first," he'd said, handing it over, "in a glass of ice water. Then you'll know it reads true." Gavin had done exactly that, tapping the dial until the needle settled where ice water should put it. The nectar jar on the windowsill, left over from his mother's tea, held his pencils, and beside it sat a cold metal spoon, a nail gone brown and flaky, and a burnt match. Evidence, he called them. His exhibit.

He remembered the match from last summer, when he'd held it too long over the camp stove and the wood had gone black and would never be wood again. That was chemical. He remembered the nail on the porch railing, rusting year after year, turning into something that crumbled when you poked it. Chemical too. Both of those his teacher had called influential examples, the ones everyone copied into their notes. So bubbles, he figured, belonged on the same list.

He held the cold spoon above the pot just as the water began to boil. Bubbles climbed and burst and the water thrashed, and Gavin held his breath and counted. One, two, three. When he pulled the spoon out, the underside was dripping wet, nothing else. No rust, no ash, no new anything. Just water. The bubbles hadn't made a new substance at all. He stared at the spoon, then at the pot, then at the sloppy capital letters in his notebook.

"That's it," he said out loud. He crossed out the old line and wrote slowly, saying the words as the pen moved. "The bubbles are water vapour. Same stuff as the water, just a gas." He looked up at the steam curling toward the ceiling. "Boiling is physical. Annie is going to lose her mind." He grabbed his phone and started typing.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
Tyler ran up the walkway carrying the plate of spring rolls his mom had wrapped in foil, because tonight was the sixth-grade potluck at Mr. Saleh's house and he had been counting the hours since lunch. The garden was lush after all the rain that week, green spilling over the edges of the flowerbeds, and he could smell something garlicky and wonderful from the porch.

At the door, Adalynn's grandmother met him with both hands pressed together and a small bow. Tyler copied her without being sure he'd done it right. Then Adalynn's whole family appeared, and instead of a wave they each nodded to him, one after another, like a line of dominoes. Inside, Mr. Saleh was greeting Jackson's family with a handshake and his hand over his heart. Same doorway, different greetings. Tyler filed that away like a trading card.

He also noticed the shoe pile by the door and the tray of oranges wrapped in red paper that Jackson's dad handed to Adalynn's grandmother. Nobody opened the gift. She just held it against her chest and thanked him twice. Interesting, Tyler thought. At his house, presents got ripped open on the spot, sometimes before the giver even sat down.

The table was incredible: noodles, dumplings, rice cookers steaming like dragons, and a big bowl of soup. Tyler piled his plate and wedged himself between Jackson and Adalynn. When Jackson leaned over to grab the soy sauce, Tyler stuck his chopsticks straight down into his mound of rice so he'd have a free hand, and grabbed the last pork bun at the exact moment Jackson reached for it.

"Hey!" Jackson said. "Are you going to accuse me of stealing, or can I accuse you? Because that bun is mine."

"Finders keepers." Tyler grinned and lifted the bun high, chopsticks standing straight up in his rice like little towers.

Adalynn went quiet. She reached over and laid his chopsticks flat across the rim of his bowl, quick and gentle, the way you'd straighten a crooked picture frame.

"We don't leave them standing up in the rice," she said. "It looks like incense offered to the dead."

Tyler looked at the two pale sticks standing in the white rice and felt his ears go hot. "Oh. Sorry. I didn't know."

"It's okay. My cousin did it at a restaurant once and my aunt nearly dove across the table." Adalynn split the pork bun in half and pushed one half onto his plate. "Trade you. Half a bun for that spring roll your mom made, because I've been staring at them all night."

"Deal." Tyler handed it over, then noticed Mr. Saleh at the head of the table raising his glass.

"Before anyone eats another bite," Mr. Saleh announced, "I should tell you I signed us all up for the spring fair agriculture exhibit, and our class is growing the lettuce."

Jackson groaned. Adalynn cheered. Tyler raised his glass of lemonade so fast it sloshed.

"To lettuce," he said.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable.
story:
Paige sat at the kitchen table with a poster board, a glue stick, and a box of strawberry stickers she had bought for exactly one purpose: to make Ms. Aziz's assignment the best one in the class. The assignment was to explain something about prices, and Paige had picked strawberries. The trouble was, she did not entirely understand her own topic yet.

She flipped through her notebook to the page from last January, when her mother had sent her to the corner store for berries and the cashier had asked for almost seven dollars. Paige remembered standing there, clutching the little plastic box, deciding whether strawberries were worth that much in the middle of winter. She had bought them anyway, because her mother had an audition that night and always wanted strawberries before she sang. That flashback gave Paige an idea, and she grabbed her jacket.

Kian lived two floors down. He was in her class, and his family bought fruit from the Saturday market every single week. "Kian," Paige said when he opened the door, "how much were strawberries at the market last Saturday?" He squinted. "Like four dollars. Same as always in June." Paige wrote it down. "And how many stands were selling them?" Kian held up three fingers, then paused. "Wait. It was six. Three new stands opened just this week." He had complained about it, actually, because the crowd near the berry tables had blocked his shortcut to the honey stall.

Paige stared at her notebook until the numbers seemed to move on their own. High price in winter, almost no stands. Lower price in June, and six stands. She had been thinking that expensive berries meant sellers would stay away, but Kian's three new stands told a different story, and she changed her mind right there at his door. When the price rises, sellers offer more, because selling becomes more profitable. She said it out loud to test it. "That's the law of supply," Kian said, nodding, because Ms. Aziz had written those words on the board on Monday and Paige had copied them without understanding them until now.

Back upstairs, Paige built her poster. On one side she drew a snow-covered market with one lonely stand and a seven-dollar sign. On the other side she drew six sunny stands with baskets stacked high. Ms. Aziz would interpret the pictures as winter and summer, Paige decided, as long as she labelled them clearly, and she carefully printed the prices beside each drawing. Her little brother wandered over and pointed at the winter side. "Why only one stand?" he asked. Paige pulled him onto her lap. "Because that's when berries are scarce," she said. "Come on, you can help me stick these on. The strawberries, not your dinosaur stickers. Those guys are extinct, remember?"

He laughed and reached for the glue stick anyway, and together they pressed a whole row of red stickers across the top of the poster, one for every dollar a summer shopper would save.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Stella had saved eleven dollars for weeks, all for the snow globe at the big garage sale on Maple Street. Last year an identical one had sold for three dollars, and she had regretted not buying it ever since. She arrived at eight sharp, before the tables were even fully set up, and there it was, on the end of the driveway beside a crate of records.

The price tag read eight dollars. Stella frowned. She turned the tag over, hoping for a mistake, but the handwriting was clear.

"That's weird," said Gurnoor, who had come with her. "It was three last year."

"Maybe nobody wanted it then," Stella said slowly. She looked around. The driveway was already crowded, and people kept stopping at that end of the table, picking up snow globes, setting them down, drifting back. A woman held one up to the light and watched the glitter swirl and refract inside the glass, then put it back with a disappointed sigh.

There were four snow globes this year. Last year, Stella remembered, there had been at least fifteen, heaped in a basket nobody touched. She felt hesitant, but she asked the man running the sale anyway.

"Why are these eight dollars? They were three last summer."

"Fewer of them this time," he said. "People were fighting over them, so we put the price up."

Stella's heart sank, and then she noticed something. The four globes sat untouched for a long while. One woman walked away shaking her head. Two kids picked theirs up, saw the tag, and put them back without a word.

"Gurnoor," she whispered, "watch. Nobody's buying at eight."

At noon the man crossed out the tag and wrote five. A girl grabbed one instantly. He crossed it out again and wrote three, and the last three sold in about a minute, including the one Stella snatched. She held it tight on the walk home, shaking it so the flakes swirled.

"Ms. Horváth told my brother there's a name for that," Gurnoor said. "The law of demand."

"Then it works," Stella said, and she shook the globe again.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
story:
Addison spread her poster board across the kitchen table and frowned at it. Sun, grass, rabbit, fox. Four boxes, and she had to connect them with arrows before science class tomorrow. Mr. Reddy had said whoever explained the chain best would present it to the class, and Addison wanted that job the way some kids wanted the last slice of pizza.

She drew the sun first, a big yellow circle in the corner. Then she wrote GRASS, RABBIT, and FOX in neat boxes going up the page. She grabbed a marker and started drawing arrows from the fox down toward the rabbit, from the rabbit down toward the grass, because that was the way the animals were looking. Her hand hovered. Something felt off, but she could not say what, so she finished the arrows and went to bed.

The next morning Keagan came by so they could walk to school together. He leaned over the poster where it sat on the porch step. "Wait," he said. "Your fox is eating the rabbit, right? Because from here it looks like the grass is eating the rabbit."

Addison snatched the poster up. "It does not." But she looked again, and Keagan was right. With the arrows pointing the way she had drawn them, the energy looked like it flowed downhill, from the fox back to the sun. She flipped through her notebook, hunting for her notes from Mr. Reddy's lecture, until she found the line she had copied off the board: the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.

"So the arrow goes from the grass to the rabbit," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud, "because the grass gets eaten." She erased every arrow and redrew them, sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to fox, going up the chain. Keagan held the eraser and handed her the marker like a surgeon's assistant. "Now it says energy flows up," he said. "Like a ladder."

At school, Mr. Reddy walked the rows checking posters. He stopped at Hillary's desk first, and Addison heard him say Hillary's arrows needed flipping too. Then he reached Addison's table and nodded. "This one works. Can you explain it?"

She stood up in front of the class with the poster and told them what she had figured out, and even cited Mr. Reddy's own lecture as her source, which made him laugh. Then he asked the hard question. "What if the rabbits all disappeared?" Addison traced the chain with her finger, sun to grass to the empty spot to fox. The grass would grow wild, she said, and the fox would go hungry or leave.

After class Mr. Reddy tapped her poster. "You'll be our ambassador at the science fair," he said. "Contemporary ecologists draw their food webs exactly like this." Addison grinned, rolled up the poster, and slid it into her backpack like a sword going into its sheath.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediation usually ends with both sides agreeing on specific actions they will each take, so each person knows exactly what they promised.
story:
Gabriel stood between Wyatt and Ava in the Hendersons' backyard, where the smell of grill smoke drifted over a table of cupcakes and someone's dog was stealing a napkin off the ground. Ava's arms were crossed so tightly she looked like a knot. Wyatt wouldn't even look at her, which Gabriel had learned, after six years of friendship with both of them, was worse than yelling. He wanted to fix it before the piñata, because once the piñata broke there would be candy everywhere and nobody would listen to anybody.

"He promised to save me the corner piece of cake," Ava said, "the one with the most frosting, and then he ate it at lunch."

"It was in the fridge with my name on it," Wyatt said. "I thought it was mine."

Gabriel's first instinct was to pick a side, but he had watched Mr. Ndlovu, the neighbor everyone said was the most influential coach in the whole rec league, settle a shouting match between two players last month without blaming anyone. Mr. Ndlovu hadn't just said "shake hands and be friends." He had made each player say exactly what he would do next time. Gabriel had a theory: maybe fights ended only when both people promised something specific, so each one knew precisely what he had promised. He decided to test it.

"You two want to just be friends again?" Gabriel asked.

"Fine," Wyatt muttered, and Ava gave a shrug that did its best to conceal how much she still cared about that frosting. They drifted apart anyway, and within ten minutes Ava was telling a fourth grader the whole story of the stolen cake, with sound effects.

Gabriel hurried back. "That didn't work," he admitted. "New plan. Ava, what will you actually do next time there's cake?"

"Write 'AVA' on the box. In marker. Big letters."

"Wyatt?"

"I'll ask before I eat anything that looks too good to be mine."

They stared at each other. "Deal," Ava said, and stuck out her hand.

Just then Mr. Henderson called out, "Piñata time!" and the dog raced past with the entire napkin holder in its jaws. Wyatt laughed so hard he snorted punch out of his nose, and Ava handed him a stack of napkins like an ambassador delivering a peace treaty. Gabriel picked up the bat and said, "I get first swing, since I'm the one who fixed you two."

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: In Stanislavski's system, an actor asks what the character wants in the scene, called the objective, and plays every line trying to get it.
story:
Jace sat in the hallway outside the auditorium with his monologue pages flat on his knees. The tournament program said Dramatic Interpretation, Round Two, 1:15 p.m., and the clock on the wall said 12:50. He had run the speech twenty times that morning, and every time it came out the same way, smooth and empty, like a robot reading a grocery list.

"You sounded like a text-to-speech app," said Emy, dropping onto the bench beside him. She popped a mint into her mouth and offered him one. "I'm not being mean. I'm being your friend."

"I know," Jace said. The mint tasted like cold pennies. He stared at the page. The monologue was about a boy whose best friend had moved away without saying goodbye, and Jace could not figure out why his voice refused to care. He could articulate every word perfectly. Nobody had ever told him to slow down or speak up. The words were just dead on the page, like a photo of an extinct animal, accurate and completely without breath.

Mathieu came back from the auditorium shaking his head. "The judge in there gave the girl before me a look like he was watching paint dry, and then a kid went up and did a monologue about a broken radio, and the judge leaned forward the whole time. I nearly clapped." He flopped against the wall. "What did the radio kid have that you don't?"

Jace watched a custodian sweep the far end of the hall, back and forth, back and forth. He thought about the radio kid, about the leaning-forward judge. The good performance had not been louder or slower. Something invisible was underneath it. He flipped his page over and looked at the blank side. Maybe the words were only the top layer, and the bottom layer, the foundation, was missing. But missing how?

Ms. Berg, the coach from his school who had driven them here, was reviewing notes down the corridor. Emy jogged over and asked her something, and when she came back she was grinning. "She told me the trick her college acting teacher used. You ask what the character wants in the scene. It's called the objective. Then you play every single line trying to get it."

Jace looked at his page again. What did the boy in the monologue want? He read it once more, hunting. Not just to be sad. The boy kept mentioning the empty porch, the unfilled seat, the letter he never sent. He wanted his friend to answer him. He wanted to be answered so badly he was talking to nobody, in public, hoping the wind would carry it. That was it. That was the want.

At 1:12 the doors opened and a volunteer called his name. Jace walked to the mark on the stage, set his pages down, and did not start right away. He let a silence sit there, heavy as a held breath. Then, instead of reciting the first line, he asked it, out toward the empty back row, as if someone might be back there after all. The judge, a tired man with reading glasses, looked up from his ballot and stopped writing. Jace pressed on, line after line, asking harder each time, his hands opening and closing like he was trying to catch something that kept slipping. When he finished, the last word hung in the air a second longer than he expected, and somewhere in the third row, Mathieu whispered, "There he is."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
story:
Theo had counted the plates twice, and the math refused to work. Nine adults, nine plates, but only seven scoops of rice, and Grandmother's plate held nothing but fruit and a bowl of sabudana, which was not rice no matter how much it pretended to be. Everyone had gathered at his aunt's house for lunch, and the smell of cumin and warm dal drifted out of the kitchen so strongly that his stomach growled like a small dog.

"Grandmother, you forgot the rice," he said, sliding the pot toward her.

"I forgot nothing," she said, and popped a slice of banana into her mouth as if that settled it.

It did not settle it. Theo had noticed this before, at dinners weeks apart, and he began to wonder whether something invisible was going on, some hidden rule deciding which days Grandmother skipped rice and which days she didn't. He had a theory, but theories needed testing. On the drive home he borrowed his mother's phone, found a lunar calendar, and started hunting. The last time Grandmother had refused rice was eleven days after the new moon. The time before that, eleven days after the full moon. He scrolled further, and there it was again: the eleventh day of each half of the lunar month, like clockwork, except lunar clockwork, which was clearly fancier.

The next Saturday his friend Pearl came over, and Theo spread his notebook on the kitchen table like a detective in a movie. "Every eleven days, twice a month," he announced. "Half a lunar month on each side. That's the pattern."

"What are you two plotting?" his mother asked, setting down two glasses of juice.

"It's called Ekadashi," Pearl said, peering at his notes. "My grandma does it too. She says it's dedicated to Vishnu."

"Vishnu," Theo repeated, and something clicked into place. "So that's why she fasts! No grains, no beans, nothing like that. She's not being negligent about rice, she's following a rule on purpose. This whole time I thought she was just picky." He felt slightly foolish and extremely pleased at the same time, a combination he recommended to everyone.

The following Ekadashi, Theo decided to try it himself, just until sunset. "A half day of rest from rice," he declared at lunch, pushing his plate away with tremendous dignity. It lasted forty minutes. Then the aroma of his father's fresh chapatis drifted down the hallway, and Theo reasoned that a boy who was growing had special needs, and that tomorrow's version of himself could handle the consequences.

He converted his fast into a promise instead: next time, he would make it all the way to moonrise. His stomach gurgled its disagreement, and Pearl, who had come over to watch, laughed so hard she knocked over the juice.
